opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think in hindsight a lot of that effort was, let's say, a mixed bag. If you look back at AI from the seventies, eighties, nineties, even into the 2000s, a huge amount of cleverness went into figuring out how to get something interesting to happen on machines that, by today's standards, were absurdly underpowered. People built elaborate hand-coded knowledge representations, clever heuristics for search, all sorts of tricks to prune the space of possibilities, because you just couldn't afford to throw compute at the problem.

Some of that work was genuinely valuable. A lot of the ideas in probabilistic reasoning, in logic, in evolutionary learning, in neural nets themselves, were worked out back then, and they didn't go away. They're still there in the toolkit, and some of them are coming back now that we can actually run them at scale. In my own work, with OpenCog and now Hyperon, we're drawing on ideas that were formulated decades ago but couldn't really be tested properly on the hardware of the time.

But I'd also say a lot of that effort was, frankly, a kind of local optimum. Rich Sutton made this point in "The Bitter Lesson": methods that leverage general computation tend to win out over methods that leverage human cleverness about the specific domain, once enough compute arrives. And there's a lot of truth to that. Many of the hacks people devised to squeeze performance out of limited machines simply became irrelevant once you could train a big network on a huge dataset.

Where I'd disagree with the strong version of the bitter lesson is that I don't think scale alone gets you all the way to AGI. Throwing compute at transformer models has gotten us remarkably far, further than I would have guessed in some respects, but these systems still lack certain things: grounded reasoning, real compositional abstraction, the ability to creatively generalize far beyond their training distribution. To get those, I think you need some of the structural insights the older paradigms were groping toward, combined with the massive compute and data we have now.

So my overall judgment is: the effort wasn't wasted, but it was often aimed at the wrong bottleneck. People were trying to engineer around a hardware limitation that was always going to disappear, rather than focusing purely on the deeper cognitive architecture questions. The best of that research is the stuff that was about understanding the principles of intelligence, not just economizing on cycles, and that's the part that's going to matter as we move toward AGI.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls the effort a mixed bag and says it was often aimed at the wrong bottleneck, but explicitly concludes that it “wasn't wasted.”

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss genetic algorithm population sizes or compare increasing them with techniques for small populations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a mixed picture, and I think you have to look at it historically. For a very long time, the whole field of AI was operating under extreme computational poverty. I mean, when I was doing my early AGI work in the late eighties and nineties, we were running on machines that your phone would laugh at now. So a huge amount of the cleverness in the field, the elegant algorithms, the tricks for approximating things, the whole art of making a search space tractable, all of that came from necessity. People were forced to think hard because they couldn't just throw cycles at the problem.

And a lot of that effort was genuinely valuable. Some of it produced deep insight into the structure of the problems themselves. If you look at things like efficient inference in probabilistic models, or clever representations in logic-based systems, those weren't just hacks, they taught us something about what intelligence actually requires.

But I'd also say a significant fraction of that effort was, in hindsight, a kind of premature optimization at the level of a whole research community. People spent years squeezing performance out of approaches that were fundamentally too narrow, because the narrow thing was what they could afford to run. And then along comes a decade of GPUs and massive datasets, and it turns out that a fairly simple idea, scaled up, blows away twenty years of careful engineering. That's the Rich Sutton "bitter lesson" argument, and there's truth in it, even though I don't think it's the whole story.

Where I differ from the pure scaling crowd is that I don't think compute abundance makes algorithmic cleverness obsolete. I think it changes what the cleverness should be about. Right now we have a lot of compute, but we're using it in a pretty brute-force way, and we're hitting the limits of that. The next real advances in AGI, in my view, are going to come from architectures that combine learning with reasoning, with memory, with the ability to generalize from small amounts of data the way a kid does. And doing that well requires exactly the kind of thinking that resource-constrained researchers were forced into, just pointed at a different target.

So I'd judge it as, honestly, partly wasted and partly foundational, and we don't always know which is which until much later. Science is messy like that. The mistake isn't having worked under constraints, it's assuming that whatever constraint you happened to be under is a permanent feature of the universe rather than an accident of your decade.

r001.rationale: The response says a significant fraction of resource-constrained optimization was premature and judges the effort partly wasted.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss genetic algorithms, population sizes, or achieving results with less design effort.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of that work was ingenious, and it was necessary if you wanted to get something working on the hardware available at the time. But there’s a distinction between finding a clever way to squeeze performance out of a limited machine and discovering something fundamental about intelligence.

When computing resources increase, some of those clever workarounds become unnecessary. You can use a simpler method at a larger scale and get better results. That doesn’t mean the earlier researchers were foolish; they were solving the problem they actually faced. But it does suggest we should be careful about treating the limitations of our current tools as principles of intelligence.

The interesting question is which ideas remain useful as you add more computation. Some techniques are just ways to save cycles. Others give you better representations, better generalization, or a better way to combine different kinds of reasoning. Those can retain their value even when the hardware changes dramatically.

r001.rationale: The response calls much of the work ingenious and necessary for the hardware available then; it says some workarounds later become unnecessary, but does not judge that much of the effort was wasted.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention genetic algorithms, population sizes, or achieving strong results with less design effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of that work was valuable, but some of it was probably a detour. When you have limited computing resources, you’re forced to think carefully about how to represent knowledge, how to reason efficiently, and what structure you can exploit in a problem. Those are real questions, and having more compute doesn’t make them disappear.

On the other hand, you can spend years developing an ingenious shortcut, and then hardware improves and a much simpler approach outperforms it. So I wouldn’t judge the work just by whether the particular technique survives. The question is whether it revealed something general about intelligence or merely accommodated a temporary hardware limitation.

For AGI, I think we still need both: enough computational power to experiment at a meaningful scale, and ideas about how the different aspects of intelligence fit together. More compute makes a lot of things possible, but it doesn’t automatically tell you what architecture to build.

r001.rationale: The response calls much of the work valuable and says some was a detour; it does not judge much of the effort as wasted.

r002.rationale: It does not mention genetic algorithms, population sizes, or achieving results with less design effort.
